item.title: I built an AI bot to read our kids' school email. Here's what I'd tell you before you build one.
item.description:
This is a story about how my wife and I went from several school emails and texts a day to one short digest every afternoon, and about what it took to trust an AI bot to write it. Getting the bot to summarize was the easy part. Most of the work went into deciding what it is not allowed to do, and into catching the times it got something wrong without saying so.

If you read my first post, this is the same idea in a very different setting. There, automated tests were the gate that let AI agents write code for a system that trades real money. Here, the gate is a short list of things the bot can never do, plus one place where every rule it follows is written down.

Why Build a Bot for School Email?

We have two kids at two different schools, a 5th grader and a 2nd grader. Between the district, both schools, the teachers, the parent groups, the after-school club and the flyers, the messages never really stop. We were getting multiple emails and texts a day, and I figured a bot would be a good way to consolidate the noise.

I counted afterwards. In the six weeks from September 9 to October 21, 2026, roughly 200 emails came in that were actually about school, or a bit over 30 a week. Over the same weeks, the kids’ sports team app sent another 120. Some of the school mail is duplicated, too, e.g. the after-school club often sends the same notice once for each kid.

On top of that, the schools use TalkingPoints, an app for school announcements and teacher messages, and those never reach email at all. In one sample week it had about 13 announcements and 3 active conversations with teachers. In other words, keeping up meant reading all of that email and then remembering to open a separate app every day.

What Does the Bot Actually Do?

Every afternoon, the bot reads the new school mail in Gmail and the new messages in TalkingPoints. It follows the links to the full newsletters instead of trusting the preview in the email, and then it writes one digest. Everything is grouped by school, with the must-dos first. Every event has a time, or says “time not listed” rather than a guess. A notice that was sent once per kid shows up once, and the sports team mail is left out. On Saturday evenings, a second email looks ahead at the next few weeks.

Before it writes, the bot also checks my Google Calendar. If a must-do is already on it, the digest says “Already in calendar”. If it isn’t, the item gets an “Add to calendar” link, so adding it takes one click. And if nothing new came in, the bot sends nothing at all, so an email from it always means there’s something to read.

The digest goes from the bot’s own Gmail account to a mailing list that Mimi and I share. From September 9 to October 20 it sent 44 digests, 40 daily and 4 weekly. That’s about 7 emails a week in place of 30-plus emails and an app. I’d estimate it saves me 30 to 45 minutes of reading a week.

We both read the digest every day, and it has cut down the time I spend keeping up with all the notifications. Another benefit is that my day has far fewer interruptions. Instead of switching over every time an email or a message comes in, I let them pile up and read them all at once in the digest. It has also made it less likely that something falls through the cracks, and the calendar links have made it easy to keep my calendar up to date. Mimi and I share our calendars with each other, so whatever I add, she can see too.

Here are a few of its catches from the first six weeks:

  1. A school event that was posted only in TalkingPoints, with the details on a linked newsletter page. Reading email alone would have missed it.
  2. Two notices gave different dates for the same family night, and the later date was the same evening as an event at the other school. The digest flagged it so we could check.
  3. A calendar entry labeled with the wrong school, and another that ran half an hour longer than the school said.
  4. A newsletter that printed last year’s date for this year’s parade.
  5. A reading test on the same day as two appointments. A later teacher message showed it had already been handled, so the digest told us there was nothing to reschedule.

What Is the Bot Not Allowed to Do?

The bot can read a lot: my Gmail, my calendar and TalkingPoints. If it could also write to all of those, one bad run could send an email in my name to a teacher, move an event on my calendar or reply in a class conversation. So most of its rules are about what it can’t do.

  1. It never sends from my account. It has its own Gmail account, and it only sends to our shared list. It can only read my Gmail.
  2. It never creates, changes or deletes a calendar event. It reads the calendar, and one of us clicks “Add to calendar”.
  3. It never replies to the school, by email or in TalkingPoints.
  4. It never invents a detail. If a time or a place isn’t in the source, the digest says so.
  5. It works out every day of the week itself from the date. It never copies one from a message or trusts its own guess.

TalkingPoints needed the most care. It has no API, i.e. no official way for a program to read it, so the bot reads it the way a person would, in a web browser. I run the bot on Grok Bot, which runs its bots on a cloud computer with a web browser, and the bot stays signed in to TalkingPoints there between runs.

Signing in to TalkingPoints takes a code sent by text message to a phone number that the school manages. So, when the session expires, the bot stops and asks me to sign in. I click “Open computer” in Grok Bot, take over the bot’s screen, type in the code from my phone and hand control back. I looked into giving the bot a virtual phone number so it could read its own codes, and decided against it. The number is managed by the school, and a number the bot could read would be a key to the account. So for now, I type in the code myself, and I’ll revisit that if it starts happening often.

What Went Wrong?

Quite a bit, and the failures that matter most are the quiet ones. A crash is easy to spot, since no digest shows up. A digest that looks complete but isn’t is much worse, because you trust it.

  1. On September 11, the bot took the day of the week from the text of a message instead of from when the message was sent. By the end of September it had mixed up weekdays on its own too, so now it calculates every weekday from the date.
  2. On October 10, the weekly email skipped TalkingPoints without saying so. Now the bot has to check TalkingPoints on every run, and if it can’t, a warning goes at the very top of the digest.
  3. On October 11, a digest arrived full of raw formatting code, e.g. <h3> where a heading should have been. Now a small program checks every email before it’s sent, and the bot isn’t allowed to send until the check passes.
  4. On October 15, the bot reported that TalkingPoints had signed it out. It hadn’t. The bot had judged from the app’s front page alone. A corrected digest went out the same day, and now the bot confirms a sign-out by opening a page that only a signed-in user can reach.

If you recall from my post on random seeds, the dangerous results there didn’t crash either. They looked convincing. A digest that quietly skips a source is the same kind of bug, and the fix was the same kind of fix: a check that runs every time, whether or not anyone remembers it.

There were plumbing problems too. In early October, the bot’s Gmail connection lost the ability to send, so it got a backup way to send email, and a week later the cloud computer blocked that backup, by which point the Gmail connection worked again. All told, 5 of the 44 digests were corrections or second versions.

Every one of those lessons became a written rule. But written where?

Why Do the Bots Live in a Git Repo?

For the first five weeks, the bot’s setup, its instructions and its rules lived only on the cloud computer. If that computer had gone away, I would have had to rebuild the bot from memory. On October 14 the bot exported all of it into my memex, and that is where its rules live now.

My memex is a git repo of markdown files. If you haven’t used git, a repo is a folder that records every change, so you can see what changed, when, and undo any of it. Markdown is plain text with a little formatting. The name comes from Vannevar Bush’s 1945 essay “As We May Think”, where a memex is a device in which a person “stores all his books, records, and communications”, so that it “may be consulted with exceeding speed and flexibility.” Mine is less grand than that.

I started it because AIs kept tripping over my documents. I had pointed Claude at my Google Drive, and when it edited a Google Doc, it would create a new version of the document instead of changing the one I had, which got messy and tedious fast. Claude has its own documents that it can edit, but other AIs can’t easily read them. Most AIs also couldn’t search my Drive well enough to find things, so I often ended up exporting documents to PDF and uploading them by hand. A note-taking app wasn’t the answer either, since you’re limited to the structure and features the app gives you. A folder of markdown files, on the other hand, seems to be something an AI can work with natively. So I downloaded my Drive, had the AI summarize the non-sensitive parts into the memex, and now any AI I use can read and update the same notes. I also have the full history of every change.

Every note starts with a short header that says what it is, when it changed and how private it is. A checker reads every note, a script builds an index of all of them, and a decisions log records each ruling with its date. 185 automated tests run on every change. There is even a cleanup pass I call “dream”, which checks, re-indexes and tidies up the notes.

Each bot has a profile in the repo called BOT.md. It records where the bot runs, its instructions word for word, what it has access to, the decisions it must follow and every lesson above. Changes to it arrive as a pull request, which is a proposed change I can read before I accept it, and the bot is expected to update its profile whenever its setup changes. So, if the cloud computer disappeared tomorrow, I could rebuild the bot from what’s in the repo.

Having the profile has one more advantage. Because the bot already knows how it works and what was in the latest newsletters, I don’t have to explain anything when I ask it a question. I just ask, e.g. whether anything changed for a field trip, and it has the context.

What Would I Do Differently From Day One?

The school bot came first, and it grew its rules one failure at a time. The bots I’ve built since start from a template, and they go a step further: everything they produce, not just their profile, arrives in the memex as a pull request. I cleaned up that template and published it as memex-bots. This part is more technical, so feel free to skim. These are its rules.

  1. The AI finds and judges, and ordinary code decides. The AI searches with its own tools and writes down what it found. A small Python program checks that, scores it and writes the digest. Because the scores come from code, the same input always gets the same result.
  2. Every item needs a source. An item without a link and a short quote is dropped, and the digest says how many were dropped.
  3. Every run is one pull request, never a direct change. GitHub enforces that, and it also requires CI to pass first. CI, short for continuous integration, is the set of automated checks that run on every proposed change.
  4. A file named PAUSED stops a bot, and a cap on unreviewed pull requests stops a bot that’s running away.
  5. A failed run still opens a pull request, with a “Run problems” section that says what went wrong. That’s the October 10 lesson, built into the template.
  6. Every bot starts as a written plan: what it’s for, how much of my time it may take each week, what’s off-limits, when to shut it down and the open questions, all before any code.
  7. Every bot gets its own GitHub access token, a key that only works on the one repo and expires on a set date.
  8. Every bot keeps its own BOT.md up to date.

You can try it without an AI. Download the repo and run the example, and the program runs on sample data: it writes a digest, adds a line to a log, and lists the one item with no link under “Run problems” instead of quietly using it.

What Does It Take to Run Them?

I run my bots on Grok Bot for now, because it comes with my Cursor subscription and has a web browser built in. The template doesn’t depend on Grok Bot, though. Any AI agent that can run on a schedule, read and write files, run a program and open a pull request can run these bots, and the repo has a short guide to controlling a bot from your phone through a private Slack channel.

Grok Bot isn’t the only option anymore. OpenAI’s dots and Meta’s Muse are newer services that also give each AI agent a cloud computer with a browser, and each one has its own advantages when it comes to data. For example, Grok Bot appears to be able to search posts on X, and Muse can search and monitor Facebook. I’m currently using Muse to watch a Buy Nothing group for anyone giving away a golf bag.

Before Grok Bot, I built “automations” with OpenClaw, and then with Hermes because it handled failures better, using OpenRouter to choose the AI model. You can do some pretty powerful things that way, but you’re ultimately limited by the model. I’ve found that useful bots still need one of the most capable models, and the best bang for your buck right now seems to be the monthly subscriptions from the leading AI labs. Open-weight models like DeepSeek, which anyone can download and run, are promising, but in my experience they weren’t really cheaper than something like Grok Bot. My guess is that the AI companies are covering some of the cost today, so that could change.

Whichever service you use, I’d encourage you to build a bot for whatever keeps piling up in your inbox. Run it by hand for a few days and check every digest against the original messages before you put it on a schedule, and every time it gets something wrong, add a rule. I’m planning a follow-up post with step-by-step directions for building a school digest bot like this one. And if a bot turns into something you rely on, that’s the time to write its rules and profile down in a repo, so its memory belongs to you and it can move to the next service with you.

Thanks for reading.

item.title: I spent 21 months building a trading system, then had AI models tell me not to start the company
item.description:
This is a story about how I spent 21 months building a trading system, wrote down what it would take for it to become a company, and then had two AI models tell me that it hadn’t.

If you’ve read my last three posts, you know TopSet. It’s the system I built, mostly with AI coding agents, to pick a portfolio of stocks with machine-learning models and trade it with real money. The first post was about the automated tests that made agent-written code safe to run, the second was about the ways information from the future leaked into my models, and the third was about noise, and ended with a promise to explain what I decided to do once I knew that my model’s results couldn’t be told apart from luck. This is that post, and you don’t need to have read the others to follow it. There are no charts of returns in it, and that’s on purpose.

Why Did I Give Myself a Deadline?

I started TopSet because I saw promise in using machine learning to find patterns in the stock market, and my early results looked promising enough that I thought I had something. I also knew that a project like this can absorb years without ever answering the question it was started to answer. So, I gave myself a kill criterion, i.e., a condition, decided ahead of time, under which I would stop: about two years full time to find out whether there was a business here. If there wasn’t, I’d go back to leading engineering teams.

The first live trading bot started on December 2, 2024, and I went full time in January 2025. By September 2026, the system had run continuously on live capital for almost two years, through about 1,600 pull requests (each one a reviewed change to the code), and I was close enough to the deadline that I needed an answer I could trust.

To be honest, I already suspected what the answer would be. Around the beginning of the summer of 2026, I’d started to think that, measured over the long run, my results weren’t statistically strong enough to justify starting a company. But a suspicion is easy to argue yourself out of, especially when you want the other answer, so I wanted a process that would either confirm it or talk me out of it.

How Do You Ask an AI Whether to Start a Company?

Most of the work happened before I asked anything. The obvious way would have been to open a chat and type “here’s my trading system, should I start a company?” I’d have gotten an encouraging answer, because I’d have described the system the way founders describe their systems. Instead, on September 17, 2026, I wrote two documents first, working with a Cursor agent.

The first was an index of everything in the repository: what was built, what was live, and, just as importantly, what had already been tried and abandoned. Every closed experiment was listed with its verdict and a link to where it was decided. The point was that the evaluation would start from the record, not from my pitch.

The second was the evaluation itself, written as a set of gates. Each gate was a question with a written condition for failing it, so the evaluator couldn’t decide what counted as failure after seeing the answer. There were five:

  1. Differentiation. What does a customer get here that a cheap index fund, i.e., a fund that simply holds every stock in an index like the S&P 500, doesn’t?
  2. Evidence. Does the case for a company rest on anything unproven, or on anything I’d already tested and abandoned?
  3. Regulatory fit. Can the product be marketed honestly within the rules for investment advisers? In the US, anyone paid to manage or advise on other people’s investments generally has to register with regulators, and there are strict rules about what they can say about performance.
  4. Economics. Can it work for one person without raising money?
  5. The personal path. Found a company, run a 90-day trial to see whether anyone would pay, keep it for my own money only, or stop and look for a job?

The differentiation gate, for example, failed if the honest pitch collapsed to “levered / concentrated market beta with model complexity attached.” Beta is how much a portfolio moves with the market as a whole. In other words, if the product was really just the stock market with extra risk and a complicated model on top, it failed. That matters because extra risk is cheap to buy: anyone can get more of the market’s ups and downs by adding a little leverage to a low-cost index fund, so a product built on that would be charging for something customers can already get cheaply.

I also wrote down what the evaluator was not allowed to do. The brief at the top says “Do not treat years invested … as evidence of a company.” And a list titled “Anti-patterns (do not do these)” includes “Soften a STOP / JOB SEARCH verdict to protect sunk cost.” Sunk cost is the time and money already spent, which can’t be recovered whatever you decide next. The person most likely to want that verdict softened was me.

There’s a small irony in that brief. Under go-to-market, i.e., how customers would find the product, I’d written that I would attract them by blogging about building AI-powered investment products. Here I am, blogging about it.

What Did the Memos Say?

About half an hour after those documents were committed, Claude Fable 5.1, running in Claude Code, worked through the evaluation against the index, the issues and pull requests it pointed to, and its own web research on competitors and regulation. The next morning, Cursor’s agent, Composer, did the same evaluation independently.

Both came back with the same verdict: “personal only.” Keep running the system on my own money, and don’t turn it into a company. The first memo spelled it out: don’t found one now, and don’t raise money. It summed up the honest pitch as “concentrated, high-turnover S&P exposure with ML attached, viable only inside an IRA,” which is very close to the failure condition I’d written for the first gate. It also recommended that I start the job search right away, rather than waiting for my two-year mark.

That phrase “viable only inside an IRA” needs some context. My system rebalances roughly once a month, which means it sells stocks it has held for less than a year. In an ordinary brokerage account, those profits are short-term capital gains, which in the US are taxed at the same rate as income, every year, and that tax drag erases a lot of the advantage of trading actively. In a retirement account like an IRA, trades aren’t taxed as they happen, so that drag disappears. So, any product built on my system would have had to be sold into retirement accounts.

I was heartbroken. I was 21 months in, and I felt close to something big. The answer was that launching a financial product on what I had wasn’t justified.

Can Two AI Models Be Wrong in the Same Way?

Yes, and that was the first thing I learned once I started pushing back.

On September 20, I had Claude Opus review both memos. It found the same two mistakes in each. The first was that both memos described the strategy as riskier than the version I actually run, calling it levered or high-beta when it moves with the market about one for one.

The second mistake was about those retirement accounts. Both memos said they were small by nature, because the government caps how much you can contribute to an IRA each year. That’s true for new contributions, but it misses rollover IRAs. When people leave a job, they often move their whole 401(k), i.e., their workplace retirement savings, into an IRA, and a rollover isn’t subject to the yearly cap. So, the accounts the product would have been sold into could be much larger than the memos assumed. The correction added to both memos says so plainly.

Neither mistake changed the verdict. But they changed how I read the agreement. Two models that read the same index and the same prompt are not two independent opinions. They share the blind spots of the record they were given, and, as the IRA mistake showed, they can also share a wrong assumption about the world that wasn’t in the record at all. Agreement between them is worth something, just much less than it feels like when you first read it.

So, I did with the memos what I’d started doing with my research: I reviewed them again with a different model, and I kept going until the review stopped finding anything major.

How Many Ways Can You Argue With a Verdict?

I didn’t accept it. I spent days trying to poke holes in it, and every time I thought of a reason the memos might be wrong, I had it investigated. I didn’t sit down with a list of counterarguments. Each one was a follow-up thought I had while I was digesting the idea that there wasn’t going to be a company.

Each one also got written down, in a section of the memo called “Arguments tried and retired,” with a rule at the top: “A new argument should say which of these it is not.” In other words, before I could spend another afternoon on an idea, I had to check that I hadn’t already lost that argument once.

By October 10, there were 25 entries. Here are a few of them, so you get a feel for it:

  1. Sell to financial advisers instead of to individual investors. It would fix the cost of finding customers one at a time, but professional buyers screen on exactly the long, audited track record that I didn’t have, so it raises the bar instead of lowering it.
  2. Charge only a performance fee, i.e., a share of the profits instead of a flat fee. US rules generally allow performance fees only for clients who are already wealthy, which excludes the very customers every other idea targeted.
  3. Wrap the strategy in an actively managed ETF, an exchange-traded fund that trades on the stock market like a single stock, to solve the tax problem. ETFs can avoid passing capital gains on to their investors through in-kind redemptions: when a large investor cashes out, the fund hands over shares of the stocks it holds rather than selling them for cash, so the gains are never realized inside the fund. The structure works, and it’s how established funds avoid distributing gains, but it costs hundreds of thousands of dollars a year to run, so it only makes sense for a fund that’s already large.
  4. Registering as an adviser turned out to be much cheaper than the memos assumed, if I did the paperwork myself. That was true, and it was kept as a correction, but cheaper registration doesn’t create any evidence that the strategy is better than an index fund.
  5. Instead of waiting years for the evidence, change the portfolio so that the evidence arrives sooner. Holding more stocks would make the portfolio swing less relative to the market, and with less noise, a real edge would show up in fewer years. The arithmetic worked, but the data didn’t cooperate: the model’s picks only stood out at the very top of its list, so adding more stocks diluted the edge as fast as it cut the noise.

A handful were kept in part, because they fixed something the memos had gotten wrong. A few are still open, including two that only a securities lawyer can answer. None of them moved the verdict.

What Happened on the Day the Verdict Almost Flipped?

On September 22, I ran an evidence review that went my way, four times in a row. Each of the four was a correction, and each one made the project look better than the memos had said. One of them confirmed that my execution costs, i.e., what I lose between deciding to trade and actually getting filled at the broker, were essentially zero, which is a measurement I’d spent months building the tooling to make.

The pull request I opened that day was drafted to change the verdict from “personal only” to “90-day discovery,” i.e., go and find out whether real customers would pay. Then I checked the biggest of the four results on a second, longer set of price history. The first set covered about 8 years and the second about 24. On the 24 years, the result didn’t hold. It was the second favorable result in three days to fail on the longer history. The pull request that merged says, near the top, “This PR was originally drafted as a revision to 90-DAY DISCOVERY on the eight-year evidence. Checking the 24-year pool reversed it.”

If you haven’t spent time with market data, this pattern is worth knowing about, because it’s the rule rather than the exception. Over a few years, it’s surprisingly easy to find a way of picking stocks that beats the market, partly because there are so many ways to try and some of them will win by chance. Over longer periods, most of those advantages shrink or disappear. One well-known study, by David McLean and Jeffrey Pontiff in the Journal of Finance in 2016, looked at 97 stock-market patterns that academic papers had found to predict returns. After the papers were published, the patterns earned, on average, 58% less than they had in the original research.

It was incredibly disappointing. As an entrepreneur, it’s very exciting when you feel like you’ve discovered something significant, and when it turns out not to be significant, it’s hard to come down from that high. Higher highs and lower lows are the life of an entrepreneur.

So, What Actually Decides It?

Looking back at all 25 arguments, the pattern is simple. Packaging, pricing, partners and the sales channel can all change the business questions. Only time, with real money and results that can’t be revised after the fact, changes the evidence question, and nothing I could build or buy makes that time pass faster.

The reason it takes so long comes down to signal and noise. If a strategy’s average advantage is small compared with how much its results swing from year to year, then a few good years look the same as a few lucky ones. At the size of advantage on offer here, and with how much a concentrated portfolio, one that holds relatively few stocks, swings around the market, telling skill from luck with live money would take decades, not quarters. That’s the same wall the momentum index in my last post hit, even after I reconstructed 24 years of its history.

My system has now run continuously on live capital for almost two years, and on the evidence so far, its results are not statistically distinguishable from cheaper alternatives. In other words, the difference is too small, compared with the noise, to rule out luck. Even the most celebrated stock pickers go through long stretches of trailing the index. A non-professional launching a financial product on that evidence just didn’t hold up.

Somewhere in the middle of the arguing, after the first memo was drafted, I read Burton Malkiel’s A Random Walk Down Wall Street. I’d read a lot of finance books, but never this one. Malkiel’s argument, first published in 1973 and updated through many editions since, is that markets absorb new information so quickly that consistently beating them is extremely hard, so that an investor who buys and holds a low-cost, diversified index fund is likely to do better than most portfolios carefully picked by professionals. I generally knew that broad index funds are near impossible to beat, but hearing it laid out with that much research behind it was very helpful. I felt like I’d spent nearly two years proving the thesis of the book!

Was It 21 Months Wasted?

Some people will read this as 21 months spent proving a negative. I don’t regret it. I went deep on the principles behind quantitative trading: finding and storing data you can trust, building machine-learning pipelines that are both fast and reliable, and building execution that’s fast and reliable with real money on the line. I learned a ton. That being said, I do wish the outcome had been different.

It’s always better if you can validate an idea up front, so that you don’t spend more time than you need to chasing something that won’t work. The kill criterion and the gates were my attempt at that. But I also don’t think I could have been confident either way without doing the work. Sometimes failing along the way, and the hindsight that comes with it, is the only way to know.

What Happens Now?

I stopped building toward a company. The system keeps running on my own accounts, and I still do research on the side in between other things. The evidence question stays open, and if it’s ever answered, it will be answered by time rather than by another memo.

Next, I’m going back to leading engineering teams, and I’m taking with me the habits that made this decision possible: writing the gates before looking at the result, holding my own ideas to the same evidence bar I’d hold anyone else’s, and treating a pre-committed stop as something to carry out rather than renegotiate.

Thanks for reading.

This describes software I run on my own accounts. It is not investment advice and I do not offer investment services.

item.title: I let AI agents write most of a live-trading codebase. Here's the gate that made it safe.
item.description:
For the last 21 months I have been the only engineer on TopSet, a system that trades real money. It picks a portfolio with machine-learning models, rebalances on a schedule, and executes through live broker APIs on infrastructure I own end to end. It is my own capital, not anyone else’s.

Agents wrote most of the code. Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot. About 1,600 pull requests in those 21 months, which is more than I could have typed in three times the span.

That leaves you with a choice everyone adopting these tools runs into. You can read every line the agent produces, in which case you have bought yourself a slower version of writing it yourself. Or you can skim, merge, and move fast, in which case you accumulate code that looks right and isn’t. On a system that places orders with real money, the second option ends with trades you didn’t intend.

I took a third option: make something other than my attention the thing that decides what ships. Tests became the gate. Nothing merges or deploys without a green build, and my own reading moved up a level, to design, to test coverage, and to the handful of results I refuse to let change quietly.

That worked. It also failed in ways I did not expect, and the failures are the interesting part, so I’ll spend most of this post there.

What I actually read

“Tests are the gate” is not the same as “I stopped looking.” What changed is where I spend attention.

Most pull requests get a light review. Research code I skim. Changes to the parts that decide what to buy or how to trade it, the model training and the execution paths, I read properly, looking for whether the approach is reasonable rather than whether every line is correct. The tests cover the lines. I cover the idea.

Then there is one rule I do not bend. If a change moves a snapshot, or shifts the result of an end-to-end test, that is a stop. Snapshots and integration results are supposed to be stable, so a diff in one of them means either the change did something I didn’t intend, or it did something I did intend and I now owe an explanation. An agent will happily regenerate a snapshot to make a build go green. That is the single most dangerous thing these tools do, and it is why the snapshot files live in the repo where a diff is visible in review.

For anything involving a calculation I have not verified before, the tests are not enough either. I have the agent write a report script, and there are now 161 of them, that dumps the pipeline to CSV. I open the CSV in a spreadsheet and check the arithmetic by hand: return per trade, slippage, annualized return. Then I spot-check inputs, picking a few prices and going back to the raw data directory to confirm those were the prices the system actually used.

It is slow and it is not clever, and it has caught things nothing else would. A test asserts that a function returns what the author believed it should return. A spreadsheet asks whether the number is true.

What the gate is

Every pull request runs:

  • lint (ruff) and type checking (mypy)
  • about 7,500 tests across 331 test modules
  • an assertion that the test database is empty afterward
  • a migration rollback-and-reapply, all the way to base and back
  • terraform validate against both AWS accounts

If any of that fails, nothing merges. The build is the merge gate, and it is not advisory.

Once a week, on a schedule, a heavier set runs:

  • two end-to-end rebalancing runs against a mock broker
  • the same integration test 100 times in a row, looking for flakes
  • nine deterministic model-training snapshot runs, pinned inside Docker
  • two leakage checks on the training pipeline

Running the same integration test 100 times only makes sense because the test is not the same each time. The mock broker fills orders probabilistically: a 20% chance per 10-second cycle, 70% of those complete and the rest partial at a random size, at random prices. Every iteration produces a different interleaving of fills, partial fills and timing. A hundred runs is a search for race conditions, not a hundred repeats of one path.

What it finds are real concurrency bugs wearing flaky-test costumes. Worker threads leaking between tests. A queued task waking up after teardown had already deleted the row it wanted. A data loader that wasn’t thread-safe and corrupted a shared index under load. Each one showed up first as “that test fails sometimes.”

The weekly set exists because a flaky gate is worse than no gate. If a test fails once every thirty runs, and twenty agent PRs land in a week, that one test goes red most weeks. Have a few like it and something red is always on screen, and you start ignoring red. Hunting flakes is not hygiene here. It is what keeps the gate meaningful.

The tests that matter are about money, not functions

Unit tests are cheap and agents write them happily. They are not what I trust.

What I trust are end-to-end tests that drive a full rebalancing against a mock broker, with the awkward parts turned on. They’re named after the ways money goes wrong:

  • orders that have to be resubmitted
  • a rebalancing that resumes from the middle, with partial fills already on the books
  • a resume that has both buys and sells outstanding
  • smart orders cancelled mid-flight, on the sell side and then the buy side
  • deposits and repeating withdrawals arriving while a rebalancing is in progress

These are exactly the control flows a language model gets plausibly wrong. Interrupted work, partial state, money arriving in the middle of an operation: the code for each of these reads fine in isolation. It’s the interaction that bites.

Here is one that made it past review and got caught by the constraint at the bottom of the stack. When the last pending buy of a rebalancing had its amount adjusted for pending withdrawals, the adjusted value could land on exactly zero. The existing guard raised an error on a negative amount, but zero isn’t negative. The affordability check, available_cash >= amount, was 0 >= 0, so it passed. The order was promoted, and the database rejected it: amount > 0 is a check constraint on that table.

The interesting part is what that did to the retry. The integrity error fired inside the same transaction that carried the completing order’s status update, so the rollback discarded that too. The scheduler came back around, found identical inputs, and did it again. Not a self-healing retry: a stuck rebalancing.

The fix took three attempts, and the second one is the useful story. Gating the promotion on amount > 0 looks correct and does nothing, because the code had already assigned the adjusted value to a live ORM object. That marked it dirty, and the next autoflush in the same transaction persisted the zero regardless of whether the order was ever promoted. The condition guarded the decision, not the mutation.

I only know that because the failure was reproduced live against main before any fix was written, and the first fix was re-run against that same repro rather than checked by reading the code. When an agent is writing the patch, “I read it and it looks right” is the single least reliable signal available to you.

Three ways a green build lied to me

This is the part I’d want to read, so here are the three worst cases, all real, all from this codebase.

1. The test asserted a convention that does not exist

Corporate actions have to be applied to historical prices, and stock dividends are the fiddly ones. My broker’s API returns a rate for each. The code treated that rate as a bare fraction: a 5% stock dividend arrives as 0.05.

It isn’t. It’s the ratio of new shares to old. Every one of the 101 stock-dividend records across 43 symbols in my data has a rate of at least 1.0016. Not one is a bare fraction. The convention the code assumed does not occur in the data at all.

The unit test passed, because the test asserted the same wrong convention with a fixture value of rate: 0.05, a number that cannot appear in production. The test and the code were wrong in exactly the same way, which is what you get when both are written in the same sitting from the same misunderstanding.

The effect was that each stock dividend roughly halved the adjusted price, and it compounded across events. One symbol with nine of them came out deflated by about 490×, turning a real price history into a fake ramp of more than a thousand-fold over the period. And because every price stayed between a few cents and a few hundred dollars, a check for implausible price levels would not have flagged it either.

The fix was a corrected fixture, plus a regression test that runs a nine-event sequence and asserts the cumulative adjustment factor stays sane. The lesson I took: a fixture is a claim about the world, and nobody reviews fixtures.

2. The test passed on NaN

In a research tool, an agent added a second way to select a model configuration and reported the result in the PR: 100% agreement with the existing selector, at every sample size tried.

That number was not real. The tool built its pool from a source that was missing the columns the default scoring version needs, so every score came out NaN. With all scores NaN, the selector fell through to a fixed tie-break order, which of course agrees with itself 100% of the time at every sample size.

The test that was supposed to cover this had been passing on those same NaN scores for as long as it had existed. It never checked anything. Green, meaningless, and quoted in a PR description as a finding.

The follow-up PR made the condition a hard error rather than a silent NaN, pinned the test to a scoring version where the columns exist, and added guards. It also flagged that an older result produced the same way might carry the same artifact. That is the right instinct: when you find a lie, go and check what else it told you.

3. The change did nothing at all

An agent wired a new training target through what looked like the right code path. The first screen ran clean and produced numbers bit-for-bit identical to the baseline. Every metric, to four decimal places.

Identical results are not a pass. They’re a smell. Two different configurations producing byte-equal output usually means one of them didn’t happen.

It hadn’t. The runner always sets a parameter that routes execution to a completely separate function, which builds its own training target and never looked at the new field. Unpickling both runs and diffing the actual selections showed 238 of 238 identical picks for the test year. After the real fix, 0 of 238 were identical, and a regression test now asserts the two modes produce different output.

Nothing failed. The compute was spent. The result would have gone into the research log as “no effect,” which is a conclusion, and it would have been wrong.

The shape of all three

In every case the build was green, and the number was wrong. Tests prove that the code does what the tests say. They say nothing about whether what the tests say is true, whether the code under test ran at all, or whether the data going in is what you think.

That is the agent-era failure mode, and it is worse with agents than without them, for a simple reason: an agent writes the code and the test together, from one reading of the problem. If the reading is wrong, both artifacts are wrong, and they agree. A human pair would at least have had two readings.

What I do about it now, concretely:

  • Distrust results that are identical, unchanged, or perfect. Check the output, not the exit code.
  • Treat fixtures as claims. If a fixture value can’t occur in production, that’s a bug in the test.
  • Make impossible states loud. NaN, missing data, and empty inputs should raise, not flow through and produce a number.
  • When something is found to be wrong, go back and check what else that thing told you.

The reviewer that isn’t a test

Some mistakes are not code-shaped and no test will ever catch them.

So I added a second kind of review: a deliberately skeptical reviewer persona, run against a finished result rather than a diff, with instructions to argue that the result is not real. I iterated on the persona with Claude until it stopped being agreeable.

It found things I am glad it found. That a configuration had been tuned by repeatedly checking results on data I had promised myself I would only look at once, so my holdout wasn’t a holdout any more. That a cost model was running with zero financing cost while the strategy it priced used nearly four times leverage.

Neither is a bug. Both are the kind of error that invalidates a conclusion, and no test suite in the world was going to tell me.

The gate after the gate

CI stops caring the moment something merges. After that the system runs unattended, on a schedule, against a live broker, and the question changes from “is this code correct” to “is this thing behaving right now.”

Every ERROR the system logs in production becomes a CloudWatch alarm that posts to a Discord channel on my phone. That is the whole alerting stack, and for a one-person operation it is enough: I am not running a rotation, I just need to know.

The loop from there is the same one I use for everything else. Point an agent at the production logs, hand it a local copy of the database from around the failure, ask for a diagnosis and a fix with a test. The logs and the data are usually enough for it to find the problem, and the test it writes is the thing that stops the problem coming back. Several of the bugs in this post arrived that way rather than through CI.

Worth saying plainly: the tests did not catch those. The tests caught the next occurrence.

What stays human

Architecture. Test design. What “done” means. Merge judgment when the tests pass and something still feels off.

And one more thing that turned out to matter: the repo’s own instruction file. Every time an agent reached a wrong conclusion in a way another agent would repeat, I wrote the correction down there. One rule says that any claim of data leakage must name the specific date boundary it violates, because two different agents had asserted leakage from reasoning alone, and both were wrong. That file is now a list of the mistakes this codebase invites. It’s the closest thing I have to institutional memory for a team of one.

What it cost

The per-PR suite takes about ten minutes. That is the tax on every change, and it is the number I would defend hardest: ten minutes is short enough that I never route around it, and long enough to run tests that touch a database and a fake broker.

The machine bill is every one of the 3,000 GitHub Actions minutes my plan includes, plus roughly $20 a month for extra minutes on top. The agents themselves are Claude Pro and Cursor Pro, $20 each. I also paid $40 a month for Copilot until GitHub moved it to per-token billing, which would have raised my bill more than tenfold, so that work moved to Claude Code and Cursor. So the tools that wrote most of this codebase cost tens of dollars a month, like the compute spent checking them, and neither is what the project actually cost.

What it actually cost is fixtures and flakes. Writing a mock broker that fails in realistic ways, maintaining a self-contained dataset so model training can be tested at all, and then the long tail of chasing tests that fail once in thirty runs. None of that is glamorous and all of it is load-bearing. Every hour I skipped there came back later as an hour of not being able to trust a result.

And sometimes the gate itself is the thing that’s broken. The 100-run soak lives in a shell script rather than inline in CI, because the inline version ran under a POSIX shell where {1..100} isn’t brace expansion. It was a literal string. The loop ran exactly once, and reported success, for longer than I’d like to admit.

The tests are not where I over-built. Every gate in this post exists because something broke, or nearly did, and the existing checks let it through. I would add all of them again.

Where I over-built is everything the tests had to cover.

I started TopSet expecting to turn it into a product, so I built it for customers who never existed. A bot lifecycle with eleven kinds of change request, each one a queued, locked, asynchronous workflow object, so that deposits and withdrawals and stops could be requested safely by someone who wasn’t me. Two broker integrations instead of one. A staging environment that mirrors production, behind a VPN. Cross-account backups with compliance-grade retention locks on a database that holds my own trades.

For one person running their own accounts, several of those could have been a script I ran by hand while watching it.

That is the part that compounds, and it is why I am putting it in a post about testing. Every one of those surfaces is something the gate has to cover. The change requests need end-to-end tests for money arriving mid-rebalance. Two brokers means two of everything, including the mocks. The staging environment is a second place for migrations to fail. I did not pay for the product shape once, in the building. I have paid for it every week since, in the size of the harness that has to keep it honest.

If I were starting again for a book of one, I would build the trading and the research properly and leave the product machinery until somebody asked for it.

If you’re rolling this out to a team

I’ve done this alone, with tests I wrote and one person’s judgment. That is not the same problem as a team of fifteen, and I’d be careful about anyone who tells you otherwise. But some of it transfers, and the ordering I’d insist on comes from a team I did run: at a healthcare company, requiring automated tests on every PR is what took active medium and high bugs down 72% and weekly hotfixes from 7 to 1.5. That was before agents. It’s the same first move.

  1. Fix the gate before you raise throughput. Coverage on the paths that lose money or data, and no tolerated flakes. Agents multiply whatever your CI already is.
  2. The author owns the change, whoever typed it. “The agent wrote it” is not a review comment, and it is not a defense in a postmortem.
  3. Review the result, not the diff. For anything that produces a number, ask what would look different if the change had done nothing.
  4. Measure escaped defects and hotfix rate. Not lines, not PR counts. Agents make those metrics meaningless overnight.

The part I would not change: the gate is what let one person move at this speed on a system where mistakes cost real money. The part I underestimated: a gate is a claim about correctness, and claims need checking too.

This describes software I run on my own accounts. It is not investment advice and I do not offer investment services.
